1120: They whispered their request, then whispered it again louder, annoyed that whispering hadn't worked.
1121: They demanded, very quietly, to be let into the special collection at once.
1122: They asked in a hush for the most valuable volume, as if the shelves themselves might overhear.
1123: They circled the reading room, sighed at every open shelf, and pointed only at the one that was locked.
1124: They offered to pay for the key to the locked shelves, then for the lock, then for the shelves.
1125: They asked for the rarest reference by name, softly, so no one else would think to want it.
1126: They insisted the special collection be opened just for them, and lowered their voice grandly.
1127: They asked which book we would least like to lose, wrote it down, and underlined it twice.
1128: They asked for the book we keep behind glass, and looked hurt that the glass was locked.
1129: They asked to be left alone with the priceless manuscript, and shushed me before I could answer.
1130: They asked to read alone, then asked everyone else to leave, then asked if the building had a basement.
1131: They whispered that the special collection was calling to them, and could I please hurry up.
1132: They demanded the rarest edition and looked wounded when I asked them to fill out a slip.
1133: They asked for the treasure of our archive by its shelf number, which they somehow already knew.
1134: They looked over the whole collection and decided the only book good enough was the one we can't replace.
1135: They promised to handle our rarest book gently, then asked if it would fit inside a coat.
1136: They wanted the most important book in the building and looked disappointed it wasn't heavier.
1137: They asked for our single most precious book and glanced around as if the shelves might steal it first.
1138: They demanded the special collection unlocked and looked personally insulted by the sign-in sheet.
1139: They described the book they wanted only as 'the expensive one' and seemed sure that was enough.
1140: They asked for our most valuable old records and slipped on gloves like a true professional.
1141: They handled the oldest documents with such expert care that I almost trusted them completely.
1142: They asked only for the priceless files and treated them so tenderly I nearly apologized for the dust.
1143: They asked for the oldest file we own and turned the pages slowly, counting each one under their breath.
1144: They requested the costliest old files and cradled them in gloved hands, whispering praise to the paper.
1145: They knew exactly which records were worth the most, and touched nothing else in the whole room.
1146: They wore archival gloves they had brought themselves and asked for our single most valuable ledger.
1147: They examined our rarest documents with expert care and complimented the ink at great length.
1148: They asked for our most fragile records and held them so still I could not tell if they were breathing.
1149: They asked for the file the whole archive is famous for, then asked, casually, if we had a copy.
1150: They requested our rarest manuscript and asked if the room had a quieter corner, away from the door.
1151: They asked which records the insurers valued highest, then held only those, with reverent care.
1152: They handled our priceless files so expertly that I forgot to be suspicious until they had gone.
1153: They requested the rarest documents and quietly measured each one against the inside of their bag.
1154: They asked for our most precious records and lifted each one as if it might shatter at a rude word.
1155: They wore the gloves, praised the paper, cradled the costliest ledger, and I was almost flattered.
1156: They asked for our oldest documents and unrolled them slowly, pausing to praise the corners.
1157: They named our finest records without looking at a single label, and handled each as though it owed them money.
1158: They requested the treasures of the collection and treated them better than most people treat me.
1159: They asked for our single most precious record and studied it far longer than reading it would take.
